sections.heading: Advances in LLM-Assisted Combinatorial Optimization
sections.text: Chuyue Tian, Ling Wang * , Jingfang Chen, Rui Li, and Jianmai Shi Abstract: Combinatorial optimization (CO) concerns decision-making over discrete solution spaces under constraints and lies at the core of many complex systems across science, engineering, and society. Yet current approaches to solving CO problems still rely heavily on expert-designed solvers and manual tuning. Large language models (LLMs), trained on massive corpora, offer a promising new avenue for enhancing CO solution methods with stronger capabilities for generalization and adaptation in complex or previously unseen scenarios. Some existing surveys provide high-level taxonomies without examining solver-level methods, while others focus narrowly on specific perspectives. To fill this gap, we present a methodology-oriented synthesis of recent LLM-assisted CO work, covering three mainstream solution paradigms: mathematical programming, heuristics, and end-to-end solvers. We first develop a hierarchical taxonomy that groups existing methods by solution paradigm and, within each paradigm, further classifies them by the workflow stage and the interaction pattern through which LLMs engage with the solver. We then formalize the workflow of each paradigm, clarify the functional role of LLMs, and analyze the core techniques in key modules. We further summarize the problem domains studied in the literature and discuss representative applications. Finally, we identify current limitations and outline future directions in architecture, methodology, and problem scope. Key words: combinatorial optimization (CO); large language model (LLM); heuristic; optimization algorithm 1 Introduction Combinatorial optimization (CO) addresses decision- making over discrete solution spaces under constraints and plays a foundational role in the efficient functioning of complex systems across science, engineering, and society [1] . Its theoretical significance and broad applicability have made it a long-standing subject of major interest in both academia and industry. The difficulty of CO problems (COPs) stems from two linked factors. First, the discrete nature of decision variables limits the direct use of smooth geometry, such as gradients, Hessians, or convexity, that underpins continuous optimization. Second, from a complexity perspective, many COPs are nondeterministic polynomial hard (NP-hard), making exact optimization computationally prohibitive at scale and forcing practitioners to balance runtime and solution quality. Accordingly, several solution paradigms have emerged, including mathematical programming, heuristics, and End-to-end (E2E) learned solvers. Mathematical programming guarantees optimality or tight bounds, but depends heavily on modeling strategies. Heuristics and metaheuristics can scale well, yet their operators and control policies are often handcrafted and difficult to transfer across domains [2] . E2E learned solvers reduce online search by learning construction or decision policies offline, but often exhibit limited robustness across instance sizes, distributions, or Chuyue Tian, Ling Wang, and Rui Li are with the Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China. Overall, strong performance across paradigms still requires substantial expert intervention in modeling, algorithm design, and parameter tuning, which limits adaptability in complex, large-scale, and dynamic real-world problems. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened a new avenue for addressing this bottleneck. Owing to their ability to process natural- language specifications, synthesize executable code, and interact with external tools, LLMs are increasingly incorporated into optimization workflows as auxiliary components that support specific stages. Driven by this trend, a rapidly growing body of work has emerged on LLM-assisted CO, as illustrated in Fig. 1. These studies span the three mainstream CO paradigms introduced above. In mathematical programming, LLMs can translate natural-language requirements into formal models, thereby supporting modeling and formulation [4] . In heuristic optimization, they have been used to generate heuristic components or executable code [5] , as well as to guide search decisions during optimization [6] . More recently, LLM-based E2E approaches have also been explored, in which LLMs directly participate in iterative solution construction [7] . Collectively, these developments suggest that LLMs can intervene in CO through multiple mechanisms and at different stages of the solution process. The increasing diversity of these approaches highlights the need for a methodological organization of the field. Several recent surveys have begun to categorize LLM applications in optimization and operations research [8, 9] . However, most either adopt a high-level perspective or focus on specific subtopics, such as automated metaheuristics or evolutionary computation. As a result, a clearer account is still needed of how LLMs intervene at the solver level and what methodological trade-offs these interventions entail. At the same time, the field continues to face important open challenges, for instance, the constraint omission in LLM-assisted automatic modeling [10] . To address this need and provide a structured view of this research area, this article presents a comprehensive review of existing methods for LLM-assisted CO. Our main contributions are listed as follows. ● We provide a comprehensive review of recent progress in LLM-assisted CO, covering representative methodologies, enabling techniques, and emerging application scenarios. ● We develop a unified hierarchical taxonomy that first distinguishes three mainstream solution paradigms—mathematical programming, heuristics, and E2E solvers—and then classifies them by the workflow stage and the interaction pattern by which LLMs engage with the solver. ● We summarize related real-world applications and analyze the practical motivations and integration patterns of LLMs across representative application scenarios. ● We identify key limitations, and outline future research trends at the architecture, method, and problem levels. The overall structure of this survey is shown in Fig. 2. Section 2 reviews prior surveys on LLM- assisted CO and introduces our taxonomy. Sections 3− 5 form the core of the work, covering the three mainstream solution paradigms: LLM-assisted modeling and solver collaboration (Section 3), LLM- assisted heuristic (Section 4), and LLM-based E2E 15 10 Number of articles published by month 5 0 2022/10 2023/03 2023/05 2023/07 2023/08 2023/10 2023/11 2024/01 2024/02 2024/03 2024/04 2024/05 2024/06 2024/07 2024/08 2024/10 2024/11 2024/12 Time (year/month) 0 20 40 60 80 100 120 140 2025/01 2025/02 2025/03 2025/04 2025/05 2025/06 2025/07 2025/08 2025/09 2025/10 2025/11 2025/12 2026/01 2026/02

A first line of work surveys learning-augmented optimization and partially touches upon LLMs. Bengio et al. [3] positioned COPs as data-driven objects and summarized how learning can replace or improve handcrafted decision rules in solvers. Following this learning-to-optimize line, Tao and Chen [8] reviewed the broader transition from deep learning to LLMs, and discussed emerging LLM-based techniques for scalable, online decision making in large instances. These surveys mainly focused on learning-based methods, particularly deep learning, while also providing useful background for subsequent LLM-oriented studies. More recent surveys are more directly connected to LLM-assisted CO. Da Ros et al. [11] conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review focused on LLM- assisted CO, categorizing studies by LLM tasks, LLM architectures, CO benchmarks, and application domains. Wang and Li [9] systematized LLM use in operations research (OR) into three pipelines, covering automatic modeling, auxiliary optimization, and direct solving. These studies established valuable taxonomies for the field, while methodological aspects such as heuristic generation mechanisms and solver-in-the-loop workflows remain comparatively less emphasized. In parallel, several surveys focus on the use of LLMs to support automated algorithm and heuristic design, especially in conjunction with evolutionary computation. Liu et al. [12] surveyed LLM-based algorithm design with a taxonomy spanning LLM roles, search methods, prompting strategies, and domains, where optimization is a major application area. Zhao et al. [13] reviewed LLM-driven metaheuristic design. Other reviews specifically examine LLM- evolutionary algorithm integration [14−17] . For instance, Zhang et al. [17] proposed a three-level taxonomy for evolutionary optimization covering problem modeling, low-level components, and high-level orchestration. Together, these surveys offered rich insights into LLM- enhanced evolutionary optimization, while placing relatively greater emphasis on that subarea than on the broader CO landscape. The inference orchestration based method corresponds to an iterative closed-loop generation workflow [4, 18−21] , which is illustrated in Algorithm 1. It preprocesses the natural-language problem specification into an intermediate representation, repeatedly samples an artifact from the LLM policy conditioned on the problem specification or history, executes it in the environment, and summarizes feedback into an updated history. This forms a closed loop that progressively improves the generated artifact. The process terminates when an acceptable artifact is obtained or a predefined budget is met. N Parameter adaptation based method adopts a fine- tune-then-generate workflow [22, 23] , shown in Algorithm 2, which separates learning from deployment. It first fine-tunes the base policy on a dataset of natural-language problem specifications, modeling artifacts, and observations to obtain a trained proposal policy. For a new instance, it generates one or candidate artifacts, then selects the best one based on its confidence level. These techniques are organized into intermediate representation (Section 3.2.1), model generation (Section 3.2.2), model verification (Section 3.2.3), as well as training and data synthesis (Section 3.2.4). Inference-based methods rely chiefly on representation, generation, and verification-guided refinement, while learning based approaches center on training and data- synthesis—though the latter also draws upon generation and refinement. 3.2.1 Intermediate representation Real-world optimization descriptions are often noisy and implicit. Directly generating modeling artifacts from free text often misses constraints or drops indices. This limitation motivates explicit problem- understanding before model generation. Several studies introduce an intermediate representation as structured abstractions of entities, relations, constraint types, and scopes. They implement this idea in different ways. NL4Opt [24] separates entity recognition and formulation generation and evaluates at the declaration level. Li et al. [25] fine-tuned a constraint classifier and used templates to synthesize mixed integer linear programming (MILP) formulas. DRoC [4] decomposes CRPs into per-constraint retrieval queries, filters examples, merges contexts, and combines retrieval with self-debug. (2) Data synthesis for scaling supervision. A representative approach to direct data synthesis is ORLM [42] , which proposes OR-Instruct, a semi- automated iterative bootstrapping pipeline. Starting from a curated set of seed industrial cases, it progressively builds a large training pool of synthetic examples and then removes low-quality instances through heuristic filtering. OptMATH [45] proposes a bidirectional synthesis loop. Starting from seed data containing mathematical formulations, OptMATH generates problem instances with controllable complexity and then performs back-translation to obtain natural-language descriptions. It subsequently performs forward modeling and uses rejection sampling to retain only those pairs that remain consistent under the round trip. As shown in Table 1, SFT is a cornerstone method for adapting LLMs to target tasks, yet it often fails to eliminate constraints that appear plausible but are in fact incorrect. To address this limitation, solver-grounded learning mechanisms convert correctness into a verifiable reward, thereby offering a more reliable training paradigm. For example, SIRL fine-tunes LLMs using RL with verifiable rewards provided by external solvers [39] . The solver returns feedback signals that include syntax validity, feasibility, and solution quality. sections.heading: Heuristic  set:
sections.text: Some systems evolve diverse heuristics, either to improve robustness across instances or to specialize per-instance distribution [60–62] . These targets form a spectrum from localized modifications to full algorithmic synthesis, with corresponding differences in evaluation cost, search complexity, and interpretability. (2) Heuristic representation. Existing LLM-based generation modules largely adopt one of the two typical representations: code-only and dual-view (thought- code) representations. In the code-only setting, each heuristic is an executable program, typically a function conforming to a predefined format, and is associated with a tuple (code, score), where code denotes the program itself and score is its evaluated performance on benchmark instances [63] . A dual-view representation couples a high-level natural language “thought”, which describes the key logic of the heuristic, with its low-level executable implementation [5] . The heuristic is thus represented as (thought, code, score), and both thought and code are evolved in a cooperative manner. Empirically, evolving with thoughts jointly can improve search efficiency and final performance. The thought provides a compact semantic handle that facilitates recombination and systematic variation through prompting. Meanwhile, prompting the LLM to generate a thought first and then produce code effectively implements a chain-of-thought (CoT) process that reduces the reasoning burden. However, the design-then-code workflow can introduce semantic drift between thought and implementation, especially for complex tasks. The first strategy is specification-grounded direct synthesis, where the LLM is prompted with a task description followed by a code format. This strategy emphasizes feasibility and reproducibility by constraining inputs, outputs, and surrounding solver scaffolding. It is commonly used to generate initial heuristics without human crafted seeds. For example, EoH [5] exemplifies direct synthesis with explicit formatting and repeated sampling to obtain diverse initial heuristics. The second strategy is edit-based generation, where the LLM is asked to modify an existing heuristic. Edit- based prompts preserve working structure and focus the model on localized changes. In practice, edit-based generation appears in several different forms. (1) One form is mechanism injection, which requests new formulas, control logic, or additional terms while retaining the main workflow [64] . (2) The second form is parameter mutation, which adjusts hyper parameters and thresholds without altering the algorithmic skeleton [5] . (3) The third form

Here, may take the form of a chain of thought, a partial solution, or a search trajectory. 240 Complex System Modeling and Simulation , September 2026, 6(3): 227−252 Table 4 summarizes existing LLM-based E2E solvers under this taxonomy. 5.2 Representation-to-solution E2E Representation-to-solution E2E methods map an input instance directly to a candidate solution through a pre- trained model without explicit intermediate reasoning structures. A task-specific example is the one-shot auto- regressive TSP model of Ghimire et al. [84] , which linearizes an instance into node features and trains a decoder-only Transformer to predict the next city under a duplicate-prevention mask. Jiang et al. [90] extended this idea to text-attributed COPs: An LLM encodes task and instance descriptions, while a lightweight Transformer decodes the solution. A complementary line incorporates solver feedback during training to reduce the mismatch between locally likely token sequences and globally feasible solutions. Awasthi et al. [88] proposed iterated fine-tuning, which repeatedly samples candidates, evaluates them with an algorithmic metric, and updates the model on high-quality samples. Jiang et al. [85] similarly combined supervised distillation from solver outputs with reward optimization over constraint satisfaction and objective quality. Compared with classical solvers, these methods shift computational effort from online search to offline training and can yield fast amortized inference on recurring instance distributions. Chuyue Tian et al.: Advances in LLM-Assisted Combinatorial Optimization 241 weakness is structural: The mapping from representation to solution is only indirectly tied to feasibility, so robustness degrades under distribution shift, larger instances, or weakly aligned textual encodings. 5.3 Reasoning-driven E2E Reasoning-driven E2E methods map an input instance to a candidate solution through explicit intermediate reasoning processes. Early work mainly examines whether LLMs can perform algorithmic reasoning over graph-structured problems described in natural language. NLGraph [7] shows that chain-of-thought and in-context learning improve performance, but gains diminish as problems grow harder or larger. Iklassov et al. [91] further extended prompting into a multi-trajectory refinement procedure resembling metaheuristic exploration, yet such methods still lack strong guarantees because generated reasoning remains textual rather than executable. This motivates more structured approaches. AFL [87] formulates CO tasks in terms of constraints, objectives, and operators, and generates candidate solvers through iterative function synthesis and execution-based debugging, thereby relocating reasoning from free- form text to testable artifacts. GraphThought [86] distills solver-aligned reasoning traces into LLMs through supervised fine-tuning, while GraphArena [38] focuses on evaluating whether generated reasoning paths correspond to feasible rather than hallucinatory solutions. Multimodal prompting further alleviates representational bottlenecks: For example, visual-text integration improves CVRP solving by exposing spatial structure that plain text obscures [89] . Table 5 summarizes the typical prompt strategies used by reasoning-driven E2E solvers. Relative to representation-to-solution models, reasoning-driven E2E methods offer better interpretability, stronger opportunities for verification, and a closer connection to classical algorithmic priors. Overall, direct decoding is simpler and faster, whereas reasoning-driven E2E methods are more structured and inspectable, but neither paradigm yet matches the consistency and scalability of strong hand-crafted or hybrid solver pipelines. 6 Comparative Discussion and Paradigm

sections.heading: Selection
sections.text: 6.1 Cross-paradigm comparison LLM-assisted modeling is most suitable when correctness, auditability, and feasibility guarantees are important, and when the main difficulty lies in formulating or maintaining optimization models. Its main limitation is that many real-world objectives and constraints are only partially expressible in standard modeling languages or lead to weak and intractable formulations. LLM-assisted heuristic solving is preferable when exact optimization is too expensive but reliable evaluation remains available. It offers flexibility and scalability, yet often incurs substantial outer-loop evaluation cost and may transfer poorly across instance distributions. LLM-based E2E solving is attractive when large numbers of similar instances justify offline training and low-latency inference is essential. However, it is typically more sensitive to scale extrapolation and distribution shift, and feasibility is weaker unless explicit constraint-preserving mechanisms are incorporated. In practice, these paradigms are often complementary rather than exclusive, and hybrid pipelines may provide the best trade-off. Table 6 summarizes the major trade- offs across the three paradigms. 6.2 Problem-type statistics Beyond conceptual differences, the literature distribution across problem types also provides empirical evidence for how these paradigms are selected in practice. Figure 5 summarizes the results and shows a clear relationship between problem structure and paradigm choice. In general, COPs with compact algebraic formulations and mature solver support are more frequently addressed by modeling-oriented approaches, since solver feedback provides reliable verification and refinement signals. Problems with reusable operators or neighborhood structures are more often studied under heuristic-oriented settings, where LLM-generated operators or search strategies can be compared under fixed computational budgets. By contrast, COPs with naturally decodable solution representations and accessible supervision are more likely to attract E2E approaches, because both training and inference can be organized around sequential generation. At the same time, these statistics should not be interpreted purely as indicators of practical importance. claims.text: LLM-assisted modeling is most suitable when correctness, auditability, and feasibility guarantees are important, and when the main difficulty lies in formulating or maintaining optimization models.
LLM-assisted heuristic solving is preferable when exact optimization is too expensive but reliable evaluation remains available, offering flexibility and scalability.

LLM-based E2E solving is attractive when large numbers of similar instances justify offline training and low-latency inference is essential, but it is typically more sensitive to scale extrapolation and distribution shift.
In practice, these paradigms are often complementary rather than exclusive, and hybrid pipelines may provide the best trade-off.
